profile.campus: Quincy, Grant County, Washington (Microsoft's original Central Washington data center campus, opened circa 2006)
profile.address: F Street Southwest, Quincy, Grant County, Washington, 98848
profile.reading:
This building is part of Microsoft's Quincy, Grant County, Washington data center campus, the company's original Central Washington site and now, per GeekWire's reporting from a May 2026 20th-anniversary celebration, the anchor of what has become Washington's largest data center hub, with Microsoft as the largest operator among several tech companies that have since built there. Microsoft first opened in Quincy around 2006, drawn by what was then surplus, low-cost hydropower from the Columbia River system; GeekWire reported that advantage has diminished over the two decades since as regional droughts became more frequent, prompting Grant County's public utility district to plan roughly $260 million in new transmission line investment, toward which Microsoft has committed more than $2.6 million. At the 20th-anniversary event Microsoft awarded $210,000 in grants to local organizations, on top of the property tax revenue its campus has generated over two decades that GeekWire reported helped fund a new high school and police station in Quincy; the town's poverty rate more than halved over the ten years through 2023, dropping to 13%, a change local and national coverage (including Fox News and OPB) have both linked substantially to Microsoft's and other data center operators' presence. Roughly 350 full-time Microsoft employees work across the Quincy data center campus, a workforce nearly seven times the size of the newer, smaller East Wenatchee campus Microsoft built in neighboring Douglas County starting in 2022. Microsoft has not published which specific building on the multi-structure Quincy campus this OSM-mapped way corresponds to, nor its individual square footage or MW capacity.

Grant County PUD, the public utility district serving Quincy, has structured its roughly $260 million transmission expansion as a cost-sharing arrangement with its largest data center customers rather than spreading the full cost across residential ratepayers, with Microsoft's multi-million-dollar contribution reported as one of several such large-load agreements the district has negotiated as Columbia Basin data center demand has grown beyond what the original hydropower surplus could support.

sources.title: Microsoft Points to Quincy to Counter Data Center Backlash - But Can It Be Repeated?
A small town in Central Washington is Microsoft's answer to the data center backlash

profile.regional_context: Microsoft has operated in the Wenatchee-Quincy corridor of Central Washington since 2006, drawn originally by low-cost hydropower; the region's utilities have since had to invest in new transmission and water infrastructure, with Microsoft contributing directly to projects like a 180MW Douglas County substation and a roughly $260 million Grant County transmission expansion, as data center demand has grown faster than the original hydropower surplus.

reading.body:
Microsoft does not publish power capacity, square footage, or technical specifications at the individual data center level, disclosing only aggregate worldwide statistics. The Quincy campus is one facility within Microsoft's Central Washington region, spanning Grant County and Douglas County, and has operated since roughly 2007, making it among Microsoft's oldest hyperscale sites. No reading of technical capacity for this campus is possible from published sources.

Within Washington state, 46 data center facilities are mapped but only 2 publish individual megawatt figures, totaling 60 MW of disclosed capacity across the state. This campus ranks third by published capacity in Washington, yet Microsoft's nondisclosure policy means its actual power draw is unknown and cannot be compared to the two published figures.

The campus matters to AI infrastructure strategy as a known node in Microsoft's hyperscale footprint and as evidence of the disclosure gap that obscures actual U.S. data center capacity. Microsoft's refusal to publish site-level specifications, despite operating one of the oldest and most significant campuses in a region explicitly transformed by data center expansion, means grid planners and researchers must infer Central Washington's AI compute density from regional power procurement and local reporting rather than from operator transparency.
